Nearly five years later, the case has drawn renewed scrutiny after US authorities moved to decertify Network for Hope, the organisation responsible for coordinating organ donations in the region.The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced on August 5, 2026, that it had begun the process of decertifying Network for Hope following federal reviews that identified concerning patient-safety practices in multiple cases involving potential organ donors. I don't have an answer for him,â she said.Procedure stopped, but questions remainedHooverâs case came to wider public attention in October 2024, when NPR reported accounts from witnesses who said he had shown signs of life during preparations for organ recovery. The Guardian also reported on the incident, including the concerns raised by former employees of the Kentucky Organ Donor Affiliates (KODA), the organisation now known as Network for Hope.Former KODA employee Nyckoletta Martin and organ-preservationist Natasha Miller raised concerns about Hooverâs condition. Miller, whose work involved preserving organs after removal, reportedly witnessed Hoover thrashing and crying on the operating table. Other accounts described him moving his head and pulling his knees towards his chest.The organ retrieval was ultimately stopped after a physician refused to proceed. Rhorer said the family was not initially given a full explanation of what had happened. She later learned more about the incident after a former KODA employee contacted her in January 2024.Hoover survived, but his family has described lasting difficulties with memory and other aspects of his daily life. Rhorerâs account has since become part of a wider debate over the responsibilities of organ procurement organisations (OPOs), which coordinate donations between hospitals, potential donors and transplant centres.Federal investigation identifies wider concernsThe controversy intensified after federal authorities examined hundreds of cases handled by Network for Hope. In its August 5, 2026 announcement, HHS said the Health Resources and Services Administration had reviewed 351 cases between 2021 and 2024 in which organ donation had been authorised but ultimately did not proceed.Of those cases, 103 had concerning features, according to the department. It said 73 patients displayed neurological signs incompatible with organ donation. The review raised concerns about neurological assessments, communication between medical teams, consent practices and the classification of causes of death, particularly in cases involving drug overdoses.The findings do not mean that organs were removed from all the patients reviewed. Instead, they point to concerns about the assessments and preparations undertaken before donation could proceed. Organ recovery must follow the applicable medical and legal requirements for determining death.US authorities move to decertify Network for HopeFollowing the federal review, HHS said Network for Hope had failed to demonstrate sufficient improvement despite earlier corrective measures and monitoring. Authorities therefore began the process of decertifying the organisation, which coordinates organ procurement across Kentucky and parts of Indiana, Ohio and West Virginia.The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services issued a notice stating that its Medicare agreement with Network for Hope would be terminated on November 3, 2026, subject to the applicable process. The organisation has also said that organ recovery can proceed only after an independent healthcare provider has declared a patient dead.The regulatory action has placed renewed focus on how hospitals and organ procurement organisations communicate with families, assess neurological activity and respond when relatives or medical staff raise concerns about a patientâs condition.The United States has more than 100,000 people waiting for organ transplants, making public confidence in the donation system critical. Experts and transplant advocates have stressed the importance of investigating alleged failures thoroughly while ensuring that individual cases do not discourage people from donating organs that could save lives.For Rhorer, however, the issue remains deeply personal.
